clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant, typically pure (uncomplicated) hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by loss-of-function variants in RTN2 (reticulon 2).
RTN2 shapes the tubular endoplasmic reticulum, placing SPG12 in the ER-morphogenesis cluster of HSPs alongside spastin (SPG4), atlastin-1 (SPG3A) and REEP1 (SPG31).
Presents with insidious, progressive lower-limb spasticity, a spastic gait, brisk reflexes and extensor plantar responses, with the upper limbs and bulbar function characteristically spared.
Age of onset spans childhood, adolescence and adult life, sometimes varying widely within a single family, reflecting variable expressivity.
Cognition, vision and cerebellar function are typically normal, helping to separate SPG12 from complicated HSP subtypes.
Diagnosis rests on a pedigree compatible with dominant inheritance plus a pathogenic RTN2 variant identified on gene-panel or exome testing.
Mild reduction of distal vibration sense may be found, but a clinically significant peripheral neuropathy is not a feature of pure SPG12.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG12 is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in RTN2, encoding reticulon 2, a member of the reticulon family of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) resident proteins. Through paired hairpin transmembrane domains, reticulons curve the lipid bilayer to generate and stabilise the tubular network of the ER. RTN2 physically interacts with spastin (SPAST/SPG4), tying SPG12 into the same molecular pathway of ER-tubule formation and axonal ER maintenance that underlies several dominant HSPs. Because the very long corticospinal axons depend on a continuous, correctly shaped ER for lipid and cargo delivery, disruption of ER architecture produces the length-dependent distal axonopathy (a dying-back degeneration) of the corticospinal tracts that manifests as slowly progressive lower-limb spasticity and weakness.
additionalDifferentials: SPG4 (SPAST / spastin) - the commonest dominant pure HSP and a direct RTN2 interacting partner
SPG3A (ATL1 / atlastin-1) - early-onset dominant pure HSP, another ER-shaping gene
SPG31 (REEP1) - dominant HSP within the same ER-morphogenesis group
SPG6 (NIPA1) and SPG8 (WASHC5) - other dominant pure forms of spastic paraplegia
Dopa-responsive dystonia and primary lateral sclerosis (spastic-gait mimics)
Acquired myelopathy from cervical/thoracic cord compression or multiple sclerosis
additionalInvestigations: Targeted HSP gene panel or exome sequencing including RTN2, with copy-number analysis
MRI of the brain and whole spine to exclude compressive, demyelinating and structural causes
Nerve conduction studies and EMG to confirm the absence of a significant peripheral neuropathy
Serum vitamin B12, copper and very-long-chain fatty acids to exclude acquired or metabolic myelopathy mimics
Detailed three-generation pedigree to establish the dominant inheritance pattern
CSF examination where an inflammatory myelopathy remains a consideration
redFlags: Rapid deterioration, a sensory level or sphincter crisis suggesting an acquired compressive or inflammatory cord lesion rather than HSP
Prominent cognitive decline, ataxia, amyotrophy or visual failure pointing to a complicated subtype or alternative diagnosis
Marked asymmetry or bulbar involvement warranting reconsideration of motor neurone disease
reference.prognosis: Generally slowly progressive with a normal lifespan; many patients retain independent or aided ambulation for decades, although spasticity-related disability accrues gradually.
pitfalls: Assuming a sporadic case excludes SPG12 - de novo variants and the wide age-of-onset range can obscure the dominant pattern
Over-investigating for a peripheral neuropathy when SPG12 is fundamentally a central corticospinal disorder
Mislabelling adult presentations as primary lateral sclerosis without genetic testing
Attributing all gait change to spasticity when treatable co-morbidities such as B12 deficiency or cervical spondylosis coexist
references: Hereditary spastic paraplegia clinical review and classification
management: Manage spasticity symptomatically with antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine, focal botulinum toxin injections and intrathecal baclofen in severe cases
Maintain mobility and prevent contractures with physiotherapy, stretching programmes, gait aids and occupational therapy
Provide orthopaedic input and orthoses for lower-limb deformity
Deliver care through a multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation team with periodic review of ambulation
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant RTN2 inheritance with variable expressivity and assessment of relatives
